lessons.title: Basic pathology: how tissues react to disease
lessons.html:
What is pathology?

Pathology is the study of disease and the changes it causes in organs and tissues. These changes are called lesions. At post-mortem inspection, the meat examiner recognises lesions and helps decide whether meat is safe. Under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000, inspection decisions follow the prescribed procedures and the judgement of the responsible meat inspector or veterinarian.

Inflammation

Inflammation is the body's response to injury or infection. Classic signs are redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function. In a carcass you see:

  • Acute inflammation: red, swollen, wet tissue, sometimes with fluid or fibrin (yellow strands) on surfaces. Names end in '-itis': pneumonia (lungs), pleuritis (chest lining), peritonitis (abdominal lining), pericarditis (heart sac), nephritis (kidneys), mastitis (udder), arthritis (joints).
  • Chronic inflammation: firm, fibrous tissue, adhesions between organs or between lung and chest wall.

Other common lesions

LesionDescription
AbscessPocket of pus surrounded by a capsule
OedemaExcess watery fluid in tissues; gelatinous, wet appearance
HaemorrhageBleeding into tissues: pinpoint (petechiae) or larger patches
BruiseHaemorrhage from trauma; colour changes with age of the bruise
NecrosisDead tissue, often pale or discoloured
Neoplasm (tumour)Abnormal growth, benign or malignant
CalcificationGritty, chalky deposits in old lesions
JaundiceYellow discoloration of fat and tissues

Localised versus generalised

A key question is whether a lesion is localised (limited to one area) or generalised (spread through the body, for example with signs in many lymph nodes, fever-related changes or infection in the blood). Localised lesions usually mean only the affected part is condemned; generalised conditions usually mean the whole carcass is condemned.

lessons.title: Applying pathology in meat inspection
lessons.html:
From lesion to decision

Systematic inspection

Inspection follows a set routine for each species: head and its lymph nodes, tongue, lungs and their lymph nodes, heart, liver and bile ducts, spleen, stomach and intestines, kidneys, and the carcass surfaces and lymph nodes. Each part is viewed, palpated (felt) and incised as the procedures prescribe. Organs and carcass must be matched so that findings in offal can be linked to the right carcass.

Describing lesions

Record and describe lesions precisely:

  • Location: which organ, which part.
  • Size and number: single or many, measured or compared (pinhead, pea, walnut size).
  • Colour, consistency and smell.
  • Distribution: focal, multifocal, diffuse.
  • Duration: acute (fresh) or chronic (old, fibrous).

Judgement categories

DecisionMeaning
PassedFit for human consumption
Partially condemnedAffected parts removed and condemned; rest passed
DetainedHeld for further examination or laboratory tests
Conditionally passedPassed after treatment, for example freezing for some parasite conditions, where the regulations allow
Totally condemnedWhole carcass and offal unfit

Examples

  • A single abscess in the liver with no other lesions: condemn the liver; the carcass may be passed.
  • Many abscesses in different parts with enlarged lymph nodes throughout: generalised infection, likely total condemnation.
  • Recent bruising on a hindquarter: trim and condemn the bruised tissue.
  • Generalised jaundice or fever-related changes: carcass is detained and usually condemned.

Safety and zoonoses

Some lesions indicate diseases that infect people, such as tuberculosis or brucellosis. Wear PPE, avoid cutting into lesions unnecessarily, sterilise knives after cutting any lesion and wash hands. Report suspected notifiable diseases to the responsible official at once.

Key points

  • Lesions are changes in tissues caused by disease or injury.
  • Inflammation names end in '-itis'; acute is red and wet, chronic is firm and fibrous.
  • Decide whether a condition is localised or generalised.
  • Describe location, size, colour, consistency, distribution and duration.
  • Sterilise knives after cutting lesions and report suspected notifiable diseases.
